digestIntro: Two threads dominate today, and both feed your consulting lanes directly. First, generative AI is quietly rewiring the customer-service and search layer: new data shows third-party AI tools are eclipsing brand-owned chatbots, which is the clearest signal yet that your AI Search Readiness thesis extends beyond search into every intermediated brand touchpoint. Second, the international-enrolment picture keeps softening, and institutions are openly rethinking where and how they recruit — the exact strategic anxiety your higher-ed practice is built to answer.
whyItMatters: Two threads dominate today, and both feed your consulting lanes directly. First, generative AI is quietly rewiring the customer-service and search layer: new data shows third-party AI tools are eclipsing brand-owned chatbots, which is the clearest signal yet that your AI Search Readiness thesis extends beyond search into every intermediated brand touchpoint. Second, the international-enrolment picture keeps softening, and institutions are openly rethinking where and how they recruit — the exact strategic anxiety your higher-ed practice is built to answer. On the home front, the Bank of Canada looks set to hold rates, which keeps the Western Canada real-estate conversation stuck in the same waiting game, and there's a leadership change worth tracking at a B.C. institution you cover. Watch the customer-service data closely — it's your best publishing hook this week, and it lets you connect martech, governance, and search into a single POV.
audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Monday, July thirteenth, twenty twenty-six. Let's get into what actually matters for your week, because there are a couple of threads today that land right in the middle of your practice.

Let's start with the story I'd flag as your best publishing hook this week. New data out this morning shows that third-party generative AI tools are now beating brand-owned chatbots in customer service. Here's the specific finding: consumer use of third-party generative AI tools — think ChatGPT, Perplexity, the assistants people already have open — has doubled in the past year. Meanwhile, usage of company-provided chatbots, the ones brands build and pay for and put on their own websites, hasn't grown in any statistically meaningful way since twenty twenty-two. Sit with that for a second, because it's more profound than a customer-service story. What it's telling you is that the interface layer between a brand and its customers is being quietly repossessed by AI systems the brand does not own and cannot fully control. Customers aren't going to the brand's bot. They're asking their AI, and their AI is answering on the brand's behalf — accurately or not.

This is exactly the argument at the heart of your AI Search Readiness thesis, and this data lets you extend it past search into service. For years the pitch has been: audit how your brand shows up in Google AI Mode, in AI Overviews, in ChatGPT, in Perplexity, because that's where discovery is happening. This story says the same dynamic is now true for support and post-purchase interactions. If a prospective student asks ChatGPT about a university's application deadlines, or a buyer asks Perplexity about a brokerage's commission structure, the answer being served is only as good as what those models have ingested — and most institutions have done zero work to make sure that surface is accurate. That's a content piece almost writing itself: the interface layer is being intermediated, owned chatbots are a sunk cost that isn't paying off, and the real work is making your brand legible and correct inside the models people actually use. That's your lane. I'd move on it this week.

One smaller AI note to keep on your radar, more as a signal than a must-read: Google is folding its Gemini assistant into Waze, with new voice and conversational features for personalizing trips. On its own it's a consumer-app update. But it's another data point in the same pattern — the assistant layer is being pushed into every everyday utility, which means the number of AI-mediated touchpoints between people and the information they act on keeps multiplying. The more surfaces Gemini and its peers occupy, the more your Search Readiness argument compounds.

Staying close to that theme, there's a useful reality check on the marketing side. An analyst is now projecting that OpenAI's advertising business is on pace to miss its own forecast by ninety percent. OpenAI has been telling people it expects a hundred billion dollars in ad revenue by twenty thirty. eMarketer's estimate for the entire chatbot advertising market — not OpenAI's slice, the whole category — tops out at around five and a half billion dollars. That is not a rounding error. That's a twenty-to-one gap between the story and the plausible ceiling.

Why does this matter to you and the people you advise? Because there's enormous pressure right now on marketing leaders to reorganize their media strategy around AI-native advertising before it actually exists as a monetizable channel. This is the counter-narrative you can own: yes, get your brand ready to be found and understood inside AI tools — that's the Search Readiness work — but no, don't rebuild your paid media plan around chatbot ad inventory that the numbers say isn't going to materialize at scale any time soon. There's a mature, defensible position in that distinction, and it's the kind of contrarian-but-grounded take that builds thought-leadership credibility. The hype and the dollars are diverging, and a consultant who can articulate exactly where is worth listening to.

The other marketing story worth your attention is Sephora's second attempt at the UK market, which the trade press is framing — correctly, I think — as a test of its global expansion playbook. After retreating from the UK back in two thousand five, Sephora is coming back, and the interesting part is how: hyperlocal nuance, market-specific adaptation, but built on a repeatable model they're already exporting elsewhere. It's a clean case study in the perennial tension between global brand consistency and local-market relevance. If you're ever building brand-strategy material for either of your industry lanes — higher ed institutions expanding recruitment into new source markets, or real estate brands scaling across regions — this is a tidy reference for how a sophisticated operator resolves that tension.

Now to higher education, and there's a leadership change worth tracking. Capilano University has appointed Dr. Vicki St. Pierre as its new Provost and Vice-President Academic. She comes over from Mount Allison. A provost move is not a ceremonial reshuffle — the provost owns academic programming and, by extension, a big share of the levers that drive enrolment strategy and institutional brand. When a B.C. institution changes its senior academic leadership, it's often a leading indicator of programming shifts and recruitment repositioning to come. Worth keeping an eye on how the mandate takes shape.

Zooming out to the sector as a whole, Inside Higher Ed published new data on international student enrolment, and the headline is that as international numbers drop, institutions are actively re-evaluating where and how they recruit. This is the strategic anxiety your higher-ed practice exists to answer. When source markets soften — and we've seen this repeatedly in recent coverage, from declining Indian demand to shifting patterns out of China — institutions are forced to diversify channels, rethink agent relationships, and reallocate recruitment budgets under pressure. The uncomfortable truth for a lot of enrolment offices is that they built their machine for a demand environment that no longer exists, and retooling it is exactly where outside strategic help earns its keep.

There's a complementary piece on the retention side that I found genuinely interesting. Ferrum College ran a program called STAR that requires — not invites, requires — struggling students to participate in structured support services. The early results show real gains in both retention and academic performance. The reason this matters strategically is that recruitment and retention are two ends of the same enrolment economics. When it's harder and more expensive to bring students in the front door, keeping the ones you already have becomes disproportionately valuable. Mandatory-support models are one answer, and there's a live debate about the paternalism-versus-outcomes trade-off. For anyone advising institutions on the full enrolment funnel, retention is the underpriced half of the conversation.

On real estate and rates. The Bank of Canada is now widely expected to hold its policy rate steady, according to a WSJ survey of economists. The framing I like best came from the coverage describing a turbulent month of economic data that leaves the Bank essentially back where it started. Job numbers, inflation, external shocks — a lot of noise, not much signal, and the net result is a central bank comfortable waiting. For Western Canada real estate, that means the holding pattern continues: buyers and sellers stuck in the same standoff, mortgage costs stable but not falling meaningfully, and no catalyst to unfreeze transaction volume. It's not dramatic, but it's the backdrop every conversation in the brokerage world is happening against, so it's worth knowing the expectation is a hold.

There's a related demand signal I'd file away. Trust and Will's CEO is pointing to rising financial stress reshaping how homeowners think about estate planning — specifically, financially anxious owners increasingly weighing estate plans and reverse mortgages to tap their home equity. It's a US data set, but the underlying dynamic travels: when rates stay elevated and cash gets tight, the family home becomes the balance-sheet lever people reach for. For brokerages advising older owners, that's a shift in the kinds of conversations coming through the door — less about trading up, more about unlocking equity. Worth being ahead of.

Closer to home in Kamloops. City Council is set to discuss a plan for hospital housing — accommodation tied to the hospital, part of the ongoing local effort to solve the workforce and healthcare-adjacent housing squeeze. It's the kind of municipal file that quietly shapes both the local labour market and the residential picture, so it's on my watch list for you.

On the public-safety side, a man has been jailed after what the courts described as a brutal Kamloops beating that left a homeless victim with brain injuries. It's the latest in a run of local violent-crime cases we've tracked, and it feeds the broader community conversation about safety and vulnerable populations that's been running through Kamloops coverage all summer.

A couple of significant world stories to be aware of. Overnight, a fast-moving fire tore through a music bar in Bangkok, killing at least twenty-seven people and leaving twenty-five in critical condition. It's shaping up as one of the deadliest venue fires of the year, and it will almost certainly reignite the global conversation about occupancy limits and fire-safety enforcement in nightlife spaces.

And closer to home, Toronto's CN Tower went dark in tribute after a shooting at the Salsa on St. Clair street festival left two people dead. Beyond the tragedy itself, expect renewed scrutiny of event and festival security across Canadian cities heading into the peak of the summer event season. If any of your family or network is attending large public events in the coming weeks, it's a reasonable prompt to be a bit more situationally aware.

Two items from the medical press worth your attention, both from STAT News. First, and this is a genuinely notable one: specialists are describing a breakthrough in pancreatic cancer — a drug called daraxonrasib — as the biggest advance in the field in decades. Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest and most treatment-resistant cancers there is, so any real progress matters. The caveat the experts themselves are raising is the standard next-chapter concern: resistance, durability, and access. But this is meaningfully good news in a space that rarely gets any.

Second, US Health and Human Services is pressing ahead with an effort to curb antidepressant use. Officials met privately with mental-health professionals to start drafting clinical guidance on how to safely stop SSRIs — so-called deprescribing. This is worth watching carefully, because it sits at the intersection of legitimate clinical concern about long-term use and withdrawal, and a broader policy posture toward psychiatric medication that some clinicians are uneasy about. If it results in credible, evidence-based withdrawal guidance, that's genuinely useful for the millions of people on these drugs. The framing and the motivation are what to watch.

And one family-safety note to close the substance. A new paper in the Canadian Medical Association Journal is urging doctors to consider anaplasmosis — not just Lyme — as tick-borne illnesses spread in Canada. Tick populations are expanding into regions that historically didn't have to think about them, and anaplasmosis presents differently enough that it gets missed. Given how much time you and your family spend outdoors around Sun Peaks and the interior, it's a small but practical reminder: tick checks after time in tall grass and brush, and if someone develops unexplained fever and fatigue after a possible bite, anaplasmosis is now on the list.

So here's where I'd put your energy this week, Midya. The customer-service AI data is your strongest content play — it takes your Search Readiness thesis and extends it into a fresh, defensible argument about brands losing the interface layer, and it pairs beautifully with the OpenAI ad reality check for a nuanced, non-hype point of view. On the client side, the softening international enrolment data and the Capilano leadership change are both reasons to lean into your higher-ed conversations right now, while institutions are visibly rethinking their playbooks. Everything else today is context — hold your rate expectations at neutral, keep an eye on the Kamloops housing file, and do a tick check. Talk soon.
